correctness.rationale: A smooth admitted plane quartic has exactly one point at infinity: in Y³Z = X⁴+aX²Z²+bXZ³+cZ⁴ the point is [0:1:0], with nonzero Z-derivative. Finite singularities are exactly common roots of f and f′ at y=0. The degree-three tame cover has five totally ramified geometric branch points, giving genus three. Counting the 500 monic squarefree quartics and taking their five-element translation orbits gives 100 centered marks. Cubing is bijective in each odd extension, forcing an even numerator by the logarithmic identity; the functional equation makes the T⁴ coefficient 5A, with A=(#C(F25)−26)/2. The factor 1+5T² is the supersingular elliptic trace-zero factor, and Tate's finite-field classification identifies the eleven different numerators with eleven different Jacobian isogeny classes (not quotients of the curves by maps). Reduction modulo five gives p-rank zero iff A=0 or 10; the claimed Newton slopes also follow from the coefficient valuations, including A=10 of valuation one. An independent direct affine-pair enumeration in F5[α]/(α²+α+1) agrees with all eleven marked multiplicities and rank totals. The independent repeated-root check over F25 is exhaustive because any repeated irreducible factor of a quartic has degree at most two.
residual_risks: Counts depend on the marking; they cannot be read as counts of curves up to isomorphism. No elliptic quotient morphisms are required or inferred.

value.rationale: F5 is the smallest base field of characteristic at least five in the nonsplit cyclotomic case q≡2 mod 3. The naturally normalized full family at this field exposes how many distinct rational isogeny types occur after odd extension counts collapse and after known rank invariants coalesce. The exact marked distribution is a useful benchmark for census and isogeny questions (for example it separates two rank-zero groups of marks with identical rank but different full numerators), rather than a recomputation of the rank locus or a sample of unrelated curves.
residual_risks: This exact minimal-field census does not provide distributions over larger fields or counts weighted by abstract isomorphism classes.
